key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: Rhode Island DCYF social workers were entitled to qualified immunity on substantive due process claims by twins abused in foster care because the evidence did not show conscience-shocking conduct, and Rhode Island sovereign and qualified immunity barred the state negligence claims.
key_cases.relevance: This case defines what a Rhode Island foster placement must look like before a caseworker's monitoring failures become constitutionally actionable.
key_cases.quote: state officials must have been at least aware of known or likely injuries or abuse and have chosen to ignore the danger to the child

key_cases.holding: A neglect decree against an incarcerated father was affirmed; findings of dependency and neglect must be made by clear and convincing evidence under Rule 17(b), and the father's inability to care for the child during an eighteen-month sentence supported the finding despite his financial provision for the household.
key_cases.relevance: It shows commitment to DCYF care, custody and control following a neglect finding against an incarcerated parent.
key_cases.quote: Based upon our review of the record, we are of the opinion that legally competent evidence exists to support the trial justice's findings of neglect.

key_cases.case_name: Hatch v. Department for Children, Youth & Their Families
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Constitution permits a Rhode Island DCYF caseworker to take temporary custody of a child without a hearing when the caseworker has a reasonable suspicion that abuse has occurred or is imminent, and the DCYF worker here met that standard, so qualified immunity barred the claim.
key_cases.relevance: A placement that follows a warrantless removal is constitutionally sound only if the initial seizure met Hatch's reasonable-suspicion test.
key_cases.quote: It follows, therefore, that a parent's right to the care, custody, and control of a minor child is inviolate unless a case worker has such a suspicion.

key_cases.holding: The dependency decree was vacated and a new trial ordered because DCYF committed an Indian child to foster placement without the qualified expert witness testimony ICWA requires and without the finding that placement with the father would likely cause serious emotional or physical damage.
key_cases.relevance: Foster placement of an Indian child without the ICWA findings is reversible error, not harmless.
key_cases.quote: In light of such disregard of ICWA requirements, we cannot say that the error was harmless.

key_cases.case_name: Sam M. ex rel. Elliott v. Carcieri
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: The district court abused its discretion in refusing to let the proposed next friends represent children in DCYF custody and in dismissing their systemic class action; the complaint was reinstated and the next friends appointed.
key_cases.relevance: The class was defined as all children in DCYF legal custody due to a report or suspicion of abuse or neglect, making this the vehicle for challenging placement practice as a whole.
key_cases.quote: We remand the case with directions to reinstate the complaint and allow Ms. Melvin, Ms. Collins, and Dr. Elliott to proceed as the children's Next Friends.

key_cases.case_name: Connor B. Ex Rel. Vigurs v. Patrick
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: Judgment on the record for the state child welfare defendants was affirmed because the foster children's class did not prove a substantial departure from accepted professional judgment under Youngberg, and class-wide liability is a precursor to any systemic injunctive relief.
key_cases.relevance: The court held that placement and kinship decisions are matters of professional judgment, so a class attack on Rhode Island placement practice must show a substantial departure from accepted professional standards rather than poor outcomes.
key_cases.quote: Not only has class-wide liability not been shown, itself a needed precursor to any relief, but plaintiffs have also not met the requirements for injunctive relief.
